exp20v2-met.three.games:
Attention, Transaction, Productivity: Which Game Is Your Product Playing?

On choosing a North Star before you choose a dashboard

Product Metrics & Measurement · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation

1. A dashboard nobody could agree on

On the second Monday of September 2026, Ananya Rao, head of product at Chakhna, a Pune-based food app, sat in a glass room with a print-out of eleven candidate metrics and no way to choose among them. Chakhna had started four years earlier as a short-video app for home cooks — recipe clips, a following-feed, a comment section regulars treated like a neighbourhood WhatsApp group. It now had 2.3 crore monthly viewers. Eighteen months in, Chakhna bolted on a grocery marketplace so viewers could buy the ingredients a video used; that surface did ₹41 crore of gross merchandise value in August. Three months ago, at the request of forty pilot restaurants who wanted to run festive-season specials the way Chakhna's creators ran recipes, the company shipped a partner dashboard: menu scheduling, inventory alerts, a demand forecast.

The dashboard was the problem. Ananya's growth lead, Neha Bhatt, in Gurugram, wanted its North Star to be weekly active restaurants — the shape of metric that had guided the video feed since year one. Her data science lead, Karthik Iyer, in Bengaluru, argued "active" meant nothing for a tool restaurants used twenty minutes a week; he wanted hours saved per restaurant per week, estimated from a time-motion study his team ran with twelve partners. A third camp, led by the restaurant-ops partner in Hyderabad, wanted GMV influenced by the dashboard, because that was the number the CFO asked about. Three metrics, three defensible stories, and a board review in five weeks where Ananya had to defend one number as the one Chakhna would manage the dashboard against. She lacked the vocabulary to explain why none of the three candidates was wrong, yet only one was right for this product.

2. The idea

A product's "game" is the kind of value exchange it asks a user to keep coming back for, and it determines what a healthy trend line looks like. The framework has no single named inventor; it crystallised through the 2010s as consumer growth teams compared notes on why a North Star that worked for one company collapsed the moment another copied it, and it was later taught under this three-way label by growth practitioners in the Reforge orbit around 2018–2020. The problem it solves is specific: a North Star metric — the single measure a team treats as the best proxy for the value it delivers — is only useful if its shape matches the shape of the value being exchanged. An attention product earns loyalty by being watched or read; a transaction product earns loyalty by completing an exchange; a productivity product earns loyalty by finishing a job of work quickly and getting out of the way. Copy the wrong shape and you optimise for something the business does not need.

The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: "A North Star has to measure the thing the user is actually trying to get, not the thing that is easy to count, and that thing differs across an attention game, a transaction game, and a productivity game."

3. How it actually works

Diagnosing the game a surface plays starts with one question, asked honestly: what does the user want less of, or more of, when the product is working? A viewer of Chakhna's recipe feed wants more — more good videos, more time well spent, more return visits driven by genuine pull. That is the attention game, and its North Star should reward volume and quality of engagement, such as minutes watched to completion per weekly active viewer. A shopper on the grocery cart wants the opposite of "more time" — a good basket built fast and paid for without friction. That is the transaction game, and its North Star should reward completed, valuable exchanges: checked-out baskets above a minimum value, not app opens. A restaurant owner using the dashboard wants less of everything except the outcome — fewer minutes on menu updates, fewer stockouts, less manual reconciliation. That is the productivity game, and its North Star should reward work finished or time reclaimed, never time spent in the tool.

The step practitioners routinely skip is checking that the metric's direction of travel matches the game. A team that inherits "sessions per week" from a consumer playbook and applies it to a B2B tool will start celebrating restaurants who visit the dashboard often — for a productivity tool, often a symptom the tool is confusing, not loved. The second skipped step is separating the North Star from its inputs: the dashboard North Star should not be "restaurants onboarded," since onboarding is an input to usage, not evidence usage created value. The third, the one boards ask about, is naming an owner and cadence — Ananya's board wanted to know not just the metric but who reviewed it weekly and what decision it changed.

4. A worked example

Karthik's time-motion study gave Ananya the raw material for a candidate North Star: hours saved per active restaurant per week. Twelve pilot restaurants were timed doing three weekly tasks — updating the festive menu, checking stock alerts, reconciling the week's Chakhna orders against their own register — first without the dashboard, then with it, over four weeks in August 2026.

Task (weekly)Time without tool (min)Time with tool (min)Minutes saved
Menu & pricing updates541638
Stock & alert checks37928
Order reconciliation632142
Total per restaurant per week15446108

Across forty pilot restaurants, that is 108 minutes × 40 = 4,320 minutes, or 72 hours, of owner and staff time saved every week — roughly 1.8 hours per restaurant. At Ananya's loaded estimate of an owner's time, ₹280 an hour for a small-format outlet, that is ₹504 per restaurant per week, or just over ₹1.05 lakh across the cohort. That number, not "weekly active restaurants," became her working North Star, with a floor of one hour to count as meaningfully active.

Ananya then ran a second pass, changing one input: what if the reconciliation task, the largest saving, breaks because Chakhna's order data stops matching a restaurant's point-of-sale export — a real risk, since only 60% of partners used a POS system Chakhna's API could read cleanly? Drop reconciliation savings to zero for the 40% on incompatible or manual registers, and the blended saving per restaurant falls from 108 minutes to about 82 — a 24% drop explained entirely by one integration gap, not by lost value everywhere. That second pass told Ananya something a single estimate could not: her North Star was fragile not to demand but to a fixable integration problem, which changed what she asked engineering to prioritise before the board review.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

A single company can play more than one game at once, and that is normal. Chakhna is not "an attention company" or "a transaction company"; it runs three products, each entitled to its own North Star, and the mistake is assuming one number should roll up cleanly across all three. Executives who ask for "one number for the whole app" are asking for something that hides more than it reveals.

Attention is not the same as engagement, and transaction is not the same as revenue. Engagement can mean confusion-driven clicking; revenue can mean one whale skewing an average. The game framework asks what behaviour the user is voluntarily repeating because it serves them — narrower and more useful than either loose synonym.

Productivity products are judged by what they let the user stop doing, which is hard to instrument. Time saved must be measured against a credible baseline, as Karthik did with the time-motion study; without one, "time in app" is all that is left to count, and it silently rewards the opposite of the product's purpose.

The three games are not always separable by product category. A payments app is usually transactional, but a savings-goal feed people check daily out of habit runs an attention game inside it, and deserves its own metric.

The game a product plays can drift over its life, and the North Star must be re-litigated when it does. Chakhna's video feed began purely attentional; once ingredient-buying became common, part of that surface started behaving transactionally, and holding onto "minutes watched" alone would have missed value created in the cart.

None of the three games tells you whether the underlying business model is sound. A transaction product can have a perfect North Star and still lose money on every order; the framework diagnoses what to measure, not whether unit economics work.

Ask, before adopting any North Star: what would this number reward if a user tried to game it — real value, or theatre? "Logins per week" rewards restaurants confused enough to keep checking; "hours saved" rewards a restaurant that barely logs in at all, uncomfortable for a board used to reading rising activity as success, but the honest answer for a productivity game.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the attention game dominates, and the trap is mistaking raw reach for depth — a video with ten times the views but one-tenth the completion rate is not obviously healthier. In B2B products the productivity game dominates, and the trap runs the other way: teams ask for consumer-style engagement dashboards because they are easier to build, even though a thriving B2B tool should show falling time-in-app once onboarding friction disappears. Marketplaces are hybrids by construction — Chakhna's grocery cart sits between viewers and local kirana suppliers — and their honest North Star is usually a transaction metric weighted by whether both sides came back, since volume alone can be propped up by one side subsidising the other. Early-stage companies should pick the North Star for the game they are betting on, even with thin data, because it shapes what a small team watches; a large company running three surfaces, like Chakhna, needs three separate North Stars with three separate owners.

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is porting a North Star wholesale from a sibling product because it is proven. The symptom is a metric reported faithfully every week that nobody acts on; the error is skipping the diagnostic in Section 3; the cheapest check is asking whether the metric would still look good if the user experience quietly got worse. The second is choosing a North Star that rewards frequency in a productivity product; the symptom is celebratory talk of "stickiness" for a tool whose users complain of complexity in tickets; the fix is a two-line survey asking whether they wish the tool took less time. The third is treating GMV or revenue as a universal fallback whenever a team cannot agree; the symptom is a headline number rising while a specific cohort — here, the 40% of restaurants without clean POS integration — quietly churns; the cheapest diagnostic is segmenting the number by cohort before presenting it.

8. What good looks like

A partner-tools team at a mid-sized logistics platform had earlier run the same diagnostic, and their board slide showed three lines on one page, clearly labelled by game, each with an owner's name and a one-line note on the decision it drove that quarter — the attention metric for their driver-app feed had triggered a redesign of a badge system inflating views without loyalty; the productivity metric for their dispatcher tool had triggered an integration fix like the one Karthik's data surfaced. Nobody asked "why three metrics" — the slide made clear each answered a different question about a different promise.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya presented hours saved per active restaurant per week as the dashboard's North Star, with a floor of one hour to count as active, paired with a secondary integrity check — the share of restaurants with clean POS integration — because the number was only honest once that gap was visible. She kept weekly active restaurants as an input metric her ops team watched, not the North Star, and GMV influenced by the dashboard as a downstream outcome reviewed monthly by finance, not weekly by product. Her reasoning matched where this page opened: the dashboard was a productivity product serving people who wanted to spend less time on Chakhna, not more, and its North Star had to reward exactly that. Her next step was building a metrics tree beneath this North Star, so the inputs feeding "hours saved" — POS coverage, alert accuracy, onboarding completion — each had an owner, because one number cannot carry a team's accountability alone. Two questions worth sitting with: when your North Star keeps rising, what would falling activity in that same number look like if the product were actually succeeding? And if a rival team inside your company asked to borrow your North Star, what would you need to know about their users first?
exp40v2-met.three.games:
Three Games, Three North Stars

Attention, transaction and productivity — and why the classification is contested, unstable and still indispensable

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

1. Two rooms, eight days apart

On the morning of 14 September 2026, Meenal Deshpande, vice-president of product at Jugnu Stories, was handed a one-page board pre-read she had not written. Jugnu was a Mumbai micro-drama studio-and-app: sixty- to ninety-second vertical episodes in Hindi, Bhojpuri, Tamil and Telugu, eight free, then coins at roughly six rupees an unlock or a ₹149 monthly pass. It had 62 lakh weekly viewers and ₹9.4 crore of net revenue in August. The pre-read, from the chief financial officer, Devesh Pai, proposed that Jugnu adopt paid unlocks per weekly viewer as its North Star — the single number the company would manage itself against — on the grounds that the category had matured, that Pocket FM and Kuku FM had taught the market to pay for serialised fiction, and that investors no longer funded minutes.

Meenal's objection was not that revenue did not matter. It was that unlocks were a consequence of something else, and that managing the consequence directly meant reaching for the paywall — the one lever guaranteed to move unlocks next week and damage the business next year. She had evidence, gathered by Ritwik Barua, her data science lead in Guwahati, and eleven days to make it an argument a board would accept.

Eight days later, Ipsita Nayak faced the inverse problem. She was head of product at Laghav Clinic Systems, a Coimbatore company whose software ran the front desk, prescriptions and billing for 4,100 small polyclinics across four states — about 13,120 doctors at ₹2,400 each per month, roughly ₹37.8 crore of annual recurring revenue. Laghav had just crossed 2,900 clinics on Laghav Sunn, an ambient AI scribe that listened to a consultation and drafted the note, billed at sixty paise a transcribed minute. It was the fastest revenue expansion in the company's history.

Yash Trivedi, the sales head in Mumbai, wanted the company North Star changed to minutes transcribed per clinic per week. It predicted the invoice, moved every day, and was already on the sales floor's wall. Ipsita's analytics lead, Bhavna Shirke in Nagpur, had pointed out what the number did when Release 9.3 shipped a bug: about six per cent of recording sessions failed silently and doctors re-recorded them. Transcribed minutes rose 5.8 per cent, adding roughly ₹18 lakh of billing. The product had got worse and the proposed North Star had gone up.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A product's game is the class of value exchange it asks a user to repeat, and three classes cover most digital products. In an attention game the user's return is itself the value: more time, of the right kind, is evidence the product works. In a transaction game value arrives in discrete completed exchanges, and time is friction on the way to one. In a productivity game the user is trying to finish a job of work and leave; the product succeeds by subtracting effort, and time-in-product is a cost the user bears, not a benefit.

The classification solves a narrow, expensive problem: teams copying North Star metrics across products whose value has different shapes. Its ancestry runs through Dave McClure's pirate metrics (2007), which gave teams a funnel vocabulary but no way to say which step was the value; Sean Ellis's single North Star; Kerry Rodden's HEART framework at Google (2010), whose "task success" dimension conceded that some products are measured by completion rather than engagement; and Croll and Yoskovitz's Lean Analytics (2013), with its six business-model archetypes and one metric that matters. The three-game label was crystallised by the Amplitude North Star Playbook lineage around 2019 and by the Reforge growth community, atop an older warning from Charles Goodhart, sharpened by Marilyn Strathern: a measure that becomes a target ceases to be a good measure.

Four schools disagree about what the classification is for, and the disagreement is not cosmetic. The behaviour-first school holds that the game is set by what the user is trying to do, and that the North Star must measure delivered user value because value leads revenue. It will sign: a metric that rises while users are worse off is disqualified, whatever it does to this quarter. It will not sign: the business model is irrelevant to metric choice. The money-first school — nearer to Lean Analytics and to aggregation-theory readings of platform economics — holds that the game is set by how the firm is paid, because that is what makes a metric actionable inside a real company. It will sign: if your pricing is per transaction, you are playing a transaction game regardless of what users feel. It will not sign: manage to revenue directly. The jobs-first school, descending from Christensen and Ulwick, holds that three categories are too coarse and that the unit of analysis is the job being hired for. The basket school, closest to HEART in practice, holds that any single number is Goodhart-vulnerable and a small, deliberately tensioned set is safer; it will not sign that a basket forces prioritisation as well as one number does.

3. Mechanics: the algebra, and the steps left implicit

Expert practice does not stop at labelling. It decomposes the candidate North Star into a multiplicative chain of inputs, because the chain is what a team can own. Written out for each game, with Jugnu's and Laghav's August 2026 numbers, the algebra looks like this.

Three steps are routinely left implicit, and they are where competent teams lose. The first is the sign test: for each input, ask whether the user would want it to rise. In Jugnu's chain a well-served viewer wants more sessions and higher completion, so both are honest inputs. In Laghav's chain the term the user wants to rise is the baseline-minus-review gap, not consults or minutes recorded; a chain whose growth depends on the user doing more work measures the firm's revenue with the user's labour.

The second is the elasticity-versus-achievability distinction. Because the chain is multiplicative, a ten per cent lift in completion rate is worth exactly as much as a ten per cent lift in sessions per viewer. Ranking inputs by mathematical leverage is therefore meaningless — every factor has unit elasticity — and the real ranking is by achievable, non-destructive delta per rupee of engineering. Ritwik's estimate was concrete: completion at 0.71 could plausibly reach 0.78 through better first-ten-second hooks, costing one squad a quarter; sessions per viewer at 4.3 could reach 4.73 only through notification pressure, which in Jugnu's own 2025 holdout cost 0.6 percentage points of weekly retention for every additional daily push. Same arithmetic contribution, opposite second-order effect.

The third is the predictive test, which decided the Jugnu argument. A candidate North Star must lead, not lag, the outcome the firm cares about. Ritwik regressed four candidates against twelve-week retention across fourteen acquisition cohorts: paid unlocks per week correlated at r = 0.21, app opens at 0.34, episodes started at 0.29, and engaged minutes — episodes watched to at least eighty per cent — at 0.68. He wrote plainly that fourteen cohorts is a small sample and the intervals overlap for the middle three, the caveat that made the finding credible in the room rather than dismissible.

4. When the classification applies, and when it misleads

Stated as testable claims, the framework holds under three conditions. One: the surface has a single dominant user role. Jugnu's feed passes — the viewer is the only actor who matters. Laghav fails badly: the doctor plays a productivity game, the front-desk operator something closer to a transaction game (patients checked in without error), and the clinic owner a third game, watching collections. One North Star for "Laghav" is a category error, and Ipsita's real task was to stop looking for one. Two: repeat usage is the value mechanism. The framework says little about one-shot products — a home-loan origination flow, a visa application, a school-admission portal. Three: the pricing model is stable enough to be ignored. Where pricing and user value pull in opposite directions, as with Sunn's per-minute billing, the classification names the conflict rather than resolving it — less than a team wants, more than it had.

The framework is actively misleading in two situations. The first is a product still discovering its game, where imposing a label early forecloses the exploration; a seed-stage team that declares itself an attention product in month four will build a feed whether or not one was warranted. The second is any product where the user's stated preference is legitimately overridden — regulated disclosure flows, clinical safety checks, know-your-customer steps mandated by the Reserve Bank. There "the user wants less time" is true and irrelevant, and a naive productivity North Star pushes a team to shave seconds off a screen the regulator requires.

5. Hard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided markets rarely play one game. Kasturi Markets, a Nashik agri trading platform, found that its buyers — institutions sourcing turmeric and chilli — play a transaction game, while farmer-producer-organisation agents uploading lots play a pure productivity game: fewer minutes per lot, fewer rejected consignments. Kasturi's answer was two North Stars reviewed together with an explicit exchange rate, because a lift on one side financed by burning the other is the classic marketplace illusion.

Regulated products place a floor under the productivity metric. Jeevika Insurance Cloud, which sells agent-facing issuance software, found that IRDAI-mandated disclosure and free-look confirmations set a hard minimum on time-to-issue; below that floor, reductions came only from skipping steps. Jeevika measures liberated time only on the discretionary portion of the flow and reports the regulated portion separately, as a constant.

Hardware-plus-software is where the classification is most often botched, as Jaltarang Devices, a Vadodara maker of connected water purifiers, botched it expensively in section 8. AI-native products create a newer seam: when inference is billed by consumption, as Sunn's is, revenue and value are structurally opposed — the firm earns more when the model needs more input, the user gains more when it needs less. Mature companies contract the seam rather than choose a side: the value metric stays the product North Star, the consumption metric moves to a finance dashboard with a named owner and a monthly cadence.

The organisational seam matters as much as the product one: an argument that looks like a measurement dispute is usually a budget dispute wearing a dashboard. Devesh Pai was not confused about attention; he was worried about a Series C in a market that had begun discounting minutes.

6. Nine nuances that separate the expert from the competent

The game belongs to a surface, not a company. The tell is an executive asking for "one number for the whole business", which an expert hears as a request for something true and useless. Jugnu runs an attention feed and a transaction storefront; Laghav runs three roles' worth of games. The obvious reading — one company, one North Star — is wrong because a North Star's job is to direct a team's weekly choices, and different surfaces face different choices.

Time-in-product is a benefit in one game and a cost in the other two. The tell is a productivity team celebrating "stickiness" while its support queue fills with confusion tickets. The obvious reading — engagement is always good — fails because longer sessions usually mean friction in a productivity game and a stalling checkout in a transaction one.

Attention metrics must carry a quality gate or they decay into volume metrics. The tell is a metric defined as "minutes" with no completion gate. Jugnu counts an episode only at eighty per cent watched; without that gate, autoplay manufactures the number. Raw minutes do not measure attention, because attention is voluntary and volume is not.

A pricing model can pull a product into a game its users are not playing, and the tension is real rather than a mistake to be argued away. The tell is a revenue metric that rises when the product regresses, as Sunn's did in Release 9.3. The expert response is not to declare the money-first school wrong but to hold both numbers, name which governs product decisions, and put the other where it cannot quietly steer a roadmap.

The game drifts, so the North Star must be re-litigated on a schedule rather than in a crisis. The tell is a metric definition document whose last edit predates the last two launches. Jugnu's feed began purely attentional; once coins arrived, a fifth of feed sessions became shopping sessions. Annual review is cheap; discovering drift in a board meeting is not.

A good North Star predicts retention; a bad one predicts this month's invoice. The tell is that nobody has ever run the correlation. The obvious reading — revenue is the most rigorous metric because it is the most audited — confuses precision with predictiveness. Jugnu's unlocks were measured to the rupee and said almost nothing about whether a cohort would still be there in December.

Productivity value requires a baseline, and the baseline is a research artefact, not a log. The tell is a team claiming hours saved without ever having timed the unaided task. Laghav's 4.6-minute baseline came from shadowing thirty-one doctors across nine clinics; Bhavna published the distribution, not only the mean, because a mean saving across a bimodal workload conceals which doctors gain nothing.

The classification is descriptive, not normative: it says what to measure, never whether the business works. The tell is a team that has diagnosed its game and believes it has therefore done strategy. A transaction product can have an immaculate North Star and lose ₹40 an order; an attention product can win minutes it cannot monetise. Turning attention into money is a separate argument needing separate evidence.

Stress-test every North Star by asking how a clever, cynical team would inflate it. The tell is that the answer arrives instantly and is something the team is already half-doing: at Jugnu, moving the paywall earlier; at Laghav, encouraging doctors to record more; at Jaltarang, adding a daily chart nobody needed. An expert runs the experiment before adopting the metric, not after the incentive has done its work.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the attention game dominates, and the recurring error is mistaking reach for depth: a Jugnu title with ten times the starts and one-tenth the completion is not the healthier asset. In business software the productivity game dominates and the error inverts — teams import consumer engagement dashboards because they are easier to build and usage charts look like success. Enterprise selling adds a complication the framework does not resolve: the buyer is not the user, and a chief medical officer signing Laghav's contract cares about audit completeness, not reclaimed doctor hours. Platforms and marketplaces are hybrids by construction, as Kasturi shows. In hardware the software's game is usually productivity or transaction, and the app should aspire to be unopened. In AI-native products the classification holds, but the consumption-pricing seam makes the money-first objection sharper than in any previous product generation.

Stage changes the answer less than people expect and the process more. A seed-stage company should choose the game it is betting on and accept it may be wrong, because a small team needs direction more than accuracy. A growth-stage company should expect one re-classification, usually when monetisation arrives. A company at Laghav's scale needs several North Stars with named owners, explicit cadences and a written statement of which decision each informs — the metrics-tree discipline most companies describe far better than they practise.

8. Three worked examples

Jugnu: two cohorts, opposite verdicts

Ritwik pulled two July 2026 cohorts of roughly 1.2 lakh users each, matched on channel and language mix, differing mainly in paywall placement.

July 2026 cohortPaywallUnlocks/user, wk 4Engaged min/user, wk 4Retention, wk 12Revenue/user, wk 12
A — Sarpanch Ki Beti (Bhojpuri)Ep 83.17134%₹212
B — Chennai Central (Tamil)Ep 44.43817%₹166

Judged on the proposed North Star, cohort B is forty-two per cent better. Judged on twelve-week revenue it is worse by ₹46 per acquired user — on equal cohorts, a gap of ₹55 lakh, and widening, since A's retention curve was still flattening while B's had flattened only because few users remained. The early paywall converted attention into cash at an exchange rate that destroyed the asset. This was Meenal's cleanest demonstration that the transaction metric was not a different view of the same truth; it ranked her options in the wrong order.

Laghav: net liberation, and the release that inverted it

Bhavna's series separated the two numbers Yash's proposal had fused.

Release (2026)Recorded min/doctor/wkReview min/consultNet liberated min/doctor/wkSunn billing/month
9.1 (June)1,2962.4376₹3.10 cr
9.2 (July)1,3011.9481₹3.11 cr

Release 9.2 improved draft quality: review time fell from 2.4 to 1.9 minutes and net liberated time rose 28 per cent while billing moved by ₹1 lakh — value created, revenue flat. Release 9.3 introduced the silent recording failure: minutes rose 5.8 per cent, billing rose ₹18 lakh, liberated time fell 11 per cent. Release 9.4 fixed it and pushed review to 1.6 minutes; liberated time reached 544 minutes a doctor a week — 9.1 hours each, 84,000 clinician-hours across 9,280 doctors — and billing fell back. No single number can be both stories, which is the whole argument.

Jaltarang: a failure and its recovery

Jaltarang Devices sold connected reverse-osmosis purifiers to 6.4 lakh households, revenue coming overwhelmingly from ₹3,600-a-year filter subscriptions. In 2024 its product team, staffed largely from consumer apps, adopted weekly active app users as the North Star and did what the metric asked: a daily water-quality feed with TDS charts, a hydration streak, push notifications. Weekly actives rose from 11 to 29 per cent of the installed base over two quarters. Service calls rose 22 per cent, because the feed made ordinary TDS variation look alarming, and renewal fell from 74 to 68 per cent — roughly 38,400 households, or ₹13.8 crore of annualised revenue. Recovery took three quarters: the team reclassified the app as productivity-plus-transaction, set the North Star to households on auto-renewing subscriptions with no unplanned service visit in ninety days, stripped the feed to threshold alerts, and accepted weekly actives falling to nine per cent. Renewal reached 76 per cent. The instructive detail is that the metric never lied; it faithfully reported that more people were opening an app they had bought a machine to avoid thinking about.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The imported North Star announces itself when a metric reported weekly has never changed a decision; the diagnostic is "what did we do differently the last time this moved?", and caught late it costs a roadmap, as at Jaltarang. The revenue-as-default failure — adopting a money metric because two teams cannot agree — shows up as a headline number rising while a named segment churns; segment before presenting. The ungated volume metric shows up as a suspiciously smooth line, since engineered volume is less noisy than real behaviour; ask what it does with autoplay off for one per cent of users. The uncontested baseline shows up as savings claims with no distribution attached; ask who in the sample gained nothing. The orphan metric — no owner, no cadence, no decision — shows up as the quarter's fourth definition of the same number, and costs most because by then two teams have optimised different things using the same word.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The behaviour-first position, at its strongest, rests on evidence like Ritwik's: user-value metrics predict retention and therefore future revenue, while revenue metrics predict only the present. It would be wrong if delivered value routinely failed to convert — if attention were, in a given market, structurally unmonetisable, a serious claim about Indian vernacular video and not obviously false.

The money-first position notes that metrics govern behaviour only if the organisation believes them, and that a number disconnected from the P&L is quietly overruled in every budget meeting. On this reading Laghav genuinely is playing a transaction game, because that is how it is paid, and liberated minutes is a research programme masquerading as management. It would be wrong if pricing models were more mutable than metrics — and Laghav could move Sunn to per-doctor pricing tomorrow, at which point the transaction framing evaporates without the user's job changing at all.

The jobs-first position holds that three games compress away the cases that matter — social products where the value is other people, safety products where the value is an event that never happens. It would be wrong if three categories explained most real North Star failures, an empirical question nobody has answered at scale. The basket school's strongest form is the observation that every case on this page shows a single metric being gamed; its weakness is that baskets of five get read as a scoreboard and prioritise nothing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks which game a surface plays before asking what to measure, and asks it of surfaces rather than companies. They can state, unprompted, how a clever team would inflate any metric they propose, and they hold a value metric and a money metric at once without pretending the tension is resolved, knowing which governs the roadmap. They re-open the classification on a calendar, not after a bad quarter. And when a number rises, their first question is whether the product got better — a habit indistinguishable from pessimism until the month it saves a business.

12. What each of them decided

Meenal proposed engaged viewing minutes per weekly viewer — episodes watched to at least eighty per cent — as the feed's North Star, with paid unlocks kept as a monitored input owned by the monetisation squad and reviewed monthly by Devesh, and the cohort table as evidence that the two numbers ranked her options in opposite directions. She conceded openly that if vernacular attention proved unmonetisable at scale, the money-first school would be right and she would be wrong. Ipsita declined to pick one number for Laghav. She set net liberated clinician minutes per doctor per week as Sunn's product North Star, moved transcribed minutes to a finance dashboard with Yash as its named owner and a monthly cadence, and commissioned a pricing review — arguing that when the billing model and the user's job point in opposite directions, the cheaper thing to change is usually the billing model.

For discussion: if Jugnu's investors continue to discount attention, at what point does Meenal's metric become denial rather than discipline? Is Ipsita's pricing review an admission that the money-first school is correct, or the only move that makes the behaviour-first school workable? And since Jaltarang's metric never lied, what should its team have been required to do before adopting it?

13. Going deeper

North Star metric is the container this topic fills: the game gives the shape, the North Star discipline says how to write, own and review the number. What makes a good metric supplies the tests — sensitivity, comprehensibility, resistance to gaming — Meenal's candidate had to pass. Vanity vs actionable metrics explains why Jaltarang's rising weekly actives felt like progress. The GAME framework turns a chosen North Star into weekly decisions. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions is where the three games diverge most, since each builds its growth loop from different materials. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio comes next: liberated minutes is a proxy, and knowing what it proxies for is the difference between using it and believing it. Breadth × depth × frequency generalises Fig. 2, and is what you will actually build the metrics tree from.

Nivesh Setu: Three Games Before Diwali

Meera Kulkarni has eleven days to decide which single number her product organisation will be judged on for the next financial year — and the answer determines whether the Diwali campaign ships at all.

1. Eleven days

At a quarter past eight on the evening of Monday, 28 September 2026, the growth review at Nivesh Setu's office in Bandra Kurla Complex, Mumbai, had run ninety minutes past its slot. Meera Kulkarni, the company's chief product officer, had on the screen in front of her a single slide titled "FY27 North Star" with three bullets and no recommendation. Her chief executive, Sandeep Varma, had asked for the recommendation by Friday, 9 October. The Diwali campaign creative locked on 16 October, and the campaign that the growth team wanted to run — a markets feed with daily streaks, a "portfolio pulse" notification at market open, and a leaderboard of the week's most-followed stocks — could only be built if the number at the top of the tree rewarded it.

Everyone in the room agreed on the facts. Nobody agreed on what the facts implied. The markets feed, shipped quietly in June as an experiment, had taken average time in app from 4.2 minutes a day to 11.6 among the users who saw it. Trades per user were up. Yet the number Meera had watched most closely for three years — the share of customers whose systematic investment plans were running without a failed mandate — had not moved at all, and among the heaviest feed users it had slipped.

2. Company background

Nivesh Setu was founded in 2018 by two former banking technologists who had watched UPI make money movement free and concluded that investing would be next. The company was a SEBI-registered stockbroker and a mutual fund distributor. Its app let a customer complete digital KYC in under seven minutes, start a systematic investment plan in a mutual fund for as little as ₹500 a month via a UPI autopay mandate on the NPCI rails, buy and sell listed shares, and — since 2023 — hold a consolidated view of holdings across the household.

By September 2026 the company had 1.9 crore registered users, 47 lakh of whom had transacted at least once in the previous twelve months. Assets under management through its mutual fund channel stood at ₹68,400 crore. Revenue for FY26 was ₹1,190 crore. It competed in a crowded and well-run market: Zerodha and Groww at scale, Angel One, Paytm Money and Upstox in the same bracket, ICICI Direct and HDFC Securities from the bank side, and a lengthening list of AMFI-registered distribution apps at the low end. Nivesh Setu's differentiation had always been the boring end of the market: households in Nashik, Coimbatore, Indore and Guwahati putting ₹2,000 a month into an index fund and never thinking about it again.

Two things had changed the strategic weather. First, SEBI's published studies on retail derivatives outcomes — which found that the overwhelming majority of individual traders in equity derivatives lost money — had made the regulator's posture toward engagement-driven trading unmistakably cautious across the whole industry. Second, Nivesh Setu had opened an NRI channel in 2025, selling through wealth advisers in Dubai and Singapore, which now contributed a disproportionate share of revenue from a very small share of users.

3. The situation

In April 2026, at the FY26 close, Nivesh Setu's revenue growth had slowed to 14 percent year on year from 41 percent the year before. Sandeep Varma had told the board that FY27 would be a year of "deepening, not widening", and a new North Star was to be chosen to express what deepening meant. The product organisation had until then run on a metric Meera had written herself in 2023: monthly customers with a healthy plan — a customer with at least one SIP mandate active, no mandate failure in ninety days, and a portfolio view opened at least once a quarter. In September 2026 that number stood at 19.4 lakh.

The markets feed had been Rohit Pillai's idea. Rohit ran growth from Bengaluru, and he had argued for two years that Nivesh Setu's users opened the app too rarely to be defended against competitors who had made investing feel alive. The June experiment gave him his evidence: time in app nearly tripled among the treatment group, trades per trading user rose from 3.1 to 5.4 a month, and week-four return visits rose eleven points.

Farida Qureshi, the company's lead data scientist in Toronto, sent Meera a note at 3 a.m. IST on 24 September that complicated the picture. She had split the treatment group by what customers actually did. Among users who came to the feed and traded, revenue per user rose sharply and twelve-month retention fell. Among users whose primary behaviour was a SIP, feed exposure correlated with a small rise in mandate cancellations — 1.4 percentage points — which Farida could not yet prove was causal but could not dismiss either. Kavya Menon, writing from Singapore, reported a third strand: her NRI customers, routed through the Dubai adviser Almas Wealth, had asked for exactly the opposite of a feed. They wanted consolidated statements, tax-ready capital gains reports and a way to see a parent's portfolio in Pune from an apartment in Deira.

4. The people

Meera Kulkarni, chief product officer, Mumbai. Eleven years in product, four at Nivesh Setu. She believes the company's durable advantage is that it is trusted with money by people who do not enjoy thinking about money. She also knows that belief is not a metric, and that her 2023 North Star has begun to feel narrow to her own team.

Rohit Pillai, senior vice-president of growth, Bengaluru. Wants time in app as the North Star, or failing that, weekly active users. His argument is competitive: attention is the scarce resource, and a product nobody opens cannot cross-sell anything. His incentive plan is weighted to user growth and revenue, not to assets under management.

Farida Qureshi, lead data scientist, Toronto. Wants whichever metric is causally cleanest and is sceptical of all three proposals. She has told Meera privately that the June experiment was not randomised properly across segments and that six weeks is too short to see mandate churn.

Kavya Menon, head of customer success, Singapore. Wants a North Star that counts completed jobs — statements delivered, gains reports filed, households linked — because those are what her NRI customers and the Dubai channel actually ask for, and because the NRI segment's revenue per user is eight times the Indian average.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Nivesh Setu revenue and gross profit by line, FY26 (₹ crore)

Exhibit 1 is the first place the three-game question gets an answer that is not a matter of taste. Forty-three percent of revenue and forty-nine percent of gross profit arrive as a trail on assets that sit still. That money is proportional to money retained, not to attention spent or to trades executed. Brokerage — the line the markets feed would move — is a third of revenue at a materially lower margin.

Retention is defined as a customer holding any asset or mandate twelve months after first transaction. Segment assignment is by dominant behaviour over the trailing six months; roughly 4 lakh customers moved segment during the period and are counted in their ending segment.

Exhibit 2 is where the argument in the room came from, because it supports both sides. Rohit's case is the revenue column: an active trader is worth ₹9,120 a year against a SIP household's ₹2,180, and active traders spend nine times as long in the app. Meera's case is the two columns either side of it: the SIP household holds six times the assets and stays twice as long, and the NRI household — 1.1 lakh customers spending four minutes a day — carries ₹14.9 lakh of assets each and renews at 94 percent. Time in app and value created are not merely uncorrelated in this table. Across the four segments they run in opposite directions once retention is taken into account.

Exhibit 3 restates Exhibit 2 in the only currency the board recognises. It should be read with its footnote in hand: the five-year figures rest on extrapolated tenure, and the NRI bar in particular is built on 1.1 lakh customers and eighteen months of history.

6. The options

Option A: the attention game. Adopt weekly minutes per active customer as the North Star, ship the Diwali feed, streaks and market-open notifications. Upside: it is the one number Rohit's team knows how to move, it defends against competitors on the dimension customers notice, and it lifts brokerage, the fastest-moving revenue line. Cost: it rewards the segment with 44 percent retention, it puts engagement-driven trading at the centre of the roadmap at a moment when the regulator's posture on retail derivatives is cautious, and it would have scored Nivesh Setu's own best feature — UPI autopay mandates that make investing invisible — as a failure.

Option B: the transaction game. Adopt monthly transacting customers or orders per customer. Upside: it is unambiguous, instrumented already, and directly proportional to 34 percent of revenue. Cost: it is indifferent to whether a transaction was wise, it ignores the trail revenue that is half the gross profit, and it makes a customer who sets one mandate and never returns look like a lapsed user rather than the company's best asset.

Option C: the productivity game. Adopt a metric that counts completed financial housekeeping — for instance monthly households with money in order: at least one mandate running without failure, portfolio reviewed once a quarter, and any pending action (KYC refresh, nominee update, capital-gains statement) cleared. Upside: it is proportional to the trail and subscription lines, it is what the Singapore and Dubai customers actually ask for, and it treats a quiet customer as a success. Cost: it is slower-moving, harder to explain to investors used to engagement charts, requires new instrumentation across three systems, and gives Rohit's team almost nothing to optimise before Diwali.

7. Questions for discussion

1. From Exhibits 1 and 2 alone, what game is Nivesh Setu's business actually playing? Which numbers in those exhibits are the strongest evidence, and which are the most misleading?

2. Rohit's June experiment is real evidence of something. Of what, exactly — and what would you need to observe over what period before it could justify a change of North Star?

3. If Meera picks Option C, what does she tell Rohit his team should work on between 16 October and Diwali? Is there a version of the campaign that serves Option C?

4. Recommend a North Star for FY27, name its owner and review cadence, and state the one decision it will trigger when it falls two periods in a row. What would make you change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a single question: which game is the product playing? A product plays the attention game when its value to the user is the experience itself and the firm is paid roughly in proportion to time spent; the transaction game when value is created at the moment an exchange completes and the firm takes a cut; and the productivity game when the product does work the user would otherwise have to do, and the firm is paid through renewal that depends on the work continuing to get done. The test that cuts through the noise is not which metric is prettier but what the firm's revenue is mathematically proportional to, followed by the question: if the outcome arrived instantly and invisibly, would the customer feel served or cheated?

Applied to Nivesh Setu, both tests point the same way for the majority of the business. Half the gross profit is a trail on assets that sit still, so revenue is proportional to money retained under management, not to minutes or to orders. And a SIP household handed a perfectly managed portfolio with no app visits at all would be delighted, not robbed. That is the signature of a productivity product. The markets feed's engagement lift is genuine, but it is a lift in a game that generates a third of revenue at the lowest margin and the worst retention in Exhibit 2.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It names the dominant game with evidence from the exhibits rather than from conviction. It refuses the false choice — engagement metrics survive, but as drivers beneath the North Star, with the direction of "good" stated explicitly and a threshold at which they become a concern. And it specifies the operating machinery: owner, cadence, and the decision the metric triggers, which is the part these programmes treat as the heart of the module and companies most often skip.

One defensible path: Meera adopts Option C, monthly households with money in order, as the FY27 North Star, owned by her and reviewed every Monday, with the rule that two consecutive months of decline triggers a roadmap review. She keeps the markets feed but re-scopes the Diwali campaign around a job rather than a streak — a "get your household's money in order before Diwali" flow that clears pending KYC refreshes, nominee updates and failed mandates, which is a productivity campaign that can still be marketed with festive urgency. Minutes per session remains on the dashboard as a driver, with the expectation stated in writing that it may fall. She gives Rohit a real prize: a co-equal driver metric of his own, browse-to-first-SIP conversion for feed users, with a threshold — if the feed does not lift new mandates by 8 percent in two quarters, it is cut rather than defended on engagement grounds. And she asks Farida for a properly randomised six-month study of mandate cancellation among feed-exposed SIP households, because the 1.4-point signal is the one number in the case that, if causal, changes everything. The reasoning is not that attention does not matter at Nivesh Setu. It is that attention is a means here and an end elsewhere, and a North Star that cannot tell the difference will mis-rank every roadmap decision for a year.

Saathi Retail Cloud: The Night Before the Board

Four point two lakh shopkeepers, three revenue lines that pull in three directions, a promise made in 2023 that nobody expected to be tested, and a term sheet that expires on 31 October.

1. Sunday night, 4 October 2026

Shalini Deshmukh's flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, was quiet at half past eleven. Her board deck was on the dining table in three printed versions, each with a different slide seven. Slide seven was titled "FY27 North Star", and in the first version it said daily billing shops, in the second weekly ordering shops, and in the third monthly reached retailers. She had written all three herself over the weekend, and she could argue any of them convincingly for twenty minutes.

The board met at ten the next morning. Devendra Kulkarni, Saathi Retail Cloud's founder and chief executive, had asked for a recommendation, not options. On Friday he had put it plainly in the corridor: "Shalini, the ad line is thirty-one crore in a quarter at ninety-one percent margin. Tell me why we would not build the business around it." She had not had a good answer then, and she did not have one now, which was not the same thing as agreeing.

On her laptop, two browser tabs were open side by side. One showed Rhea Bhattacharya's growth dashboard: Saathi Feed, minutes per retailer per day up from 2.1 in March to 9.4 in September, weekly retention up fourteen points. The other showed a spreadsheet Ananya Ghosh had sent from Toronto at 4 p.m. IST, which said that among the retailers in the top decile of Feed exposure, subscription renewal was six points lower than among the bottom decile. Ananya's covering note said the decile analysis was confounded and that she could not yet say by how much. It was the only honest sentence Shalini had read all week, and it was useless to her by ten o'clock tomorrow.

2. Company history, and a promise made in 2023

Saathi Retail Cloud was founded in 2019 in Bengaluru by Devendra Kulkarni, formerly a distribution manager at a packaged-foods company, and Farhan Shaikh, an engineer from Pune. The original product was a free Android app that let a kirana shop owner record udhaar — credit given to regular customers — and take payments by UPI. It grew by word of mouth through distributor networks in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and by 2021 had 62 lakh installs and almost no revenue.

In 2021 the company launched a paid tier: ₹1,999 a year for GST-compliant invoicing, stock management and a printable day book. It converted badly at first, because Khatabook and Vyapar offered a great deal for free and shop owners in Belagavi did not see why a ledger should cost money. The turn came in 2023, and it came from a promise.

Facing free competitors, Devendra and Shalini — then head of product — made a decision that has constrained every decision since. They wrote into the subscription terms, in eleven languages, in language the sales team could repeat on a doorstep, a commitment that the paid product would contain "no advertising in your ledger, ever". It was not a marketing line. It was in the T&Cs, clause 4.3, and the field sales team in Nashik and Coimbatore built their whole pitch on it: your shop's numbers are yours, and nobody will sell them to a brand. Paid retailers went from 38,000 to 1.4 lakh in eighteen months. Subscription price rose to ₹2,999 in 2024 and ₹3,499 in 2025.

Three later decisions matter. In 2024 Saathi launched a B2B ordering marketplace, letting shops order stock from distributors in-app; the plan assumed a 4 percent take rate and the market gave them 1.8 percent, because distributors had alternatives and margins in FMCG distribution are thin. In March 2025 Farhan's team completed a fourteen-month, ₹41 crore rewrite that made the ledger fully offline-first, on the argument that a shop in Jhunjhunu with patchy 4G would churn otherwise; churn improved by two points, less than the business case promised, while NPS rose by nineteen. And in November 2025 the company launched Saathi Feed — short vernacular videos on GST filing, festive merchandising, credit discipline — with no advertising, as a subscription-upsell device.

In April 2026 the Feed began carrying sponsored content: two-minute videos produced for brands of the sort that fill a kirana shelf, marked "Sponsored". Outside counsel in Mumbai had given a written opinion that sponsored content in a separate Feed tab was not "advertising in your ledger" within the meaning of clause 4.3. That opinion is in the board pack as an appendix. Nobody on the board has read it.

3. The industry around them

India's retail software market in 2026 was crowded at every price point. At the free end, Khatabook and Vyapar had enormous installed bases. In restaurants, Petpooja had built a specialised billing business. Upmarket, Zoho's accounting suite was the reference standard for small businesses that had an accountant. In B2B ordering, Udaan and Jumbotail had spent years teaching kirana owners to buy stock on an app, and Reliance Retail's cash-and-carry network and Metro's stores did the same job offline with wholesale pricing. ONDC had, since 2023, made it cheaper for a small seller to be discoverable without belonging to a platform, which cut both ways: it lowered Saathi's cost of building demand and lowered its ability to lock anyone in.

Three regulatory and macro facts bore directly on Shalini's slide seven. GST e-invoicing thresholds had come down far enough that a significant share of Saathi's larger retailers now had a statutory reason to bill through software — a durable tailwind for the productivity product. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, now in force, required specific, purpose-limited consent for processing personal data; Saathi's legal team had advised that using a retailer's transaction data to target brand advertising required a fresh consent flow, and that re-collecting consent from 4.2 lakh retailers in eleven languages would take roughly six weeks and would visibly re-open the question clause 4.3 had closed. And the UPI rails, free to the merchant, meant Saathi could never charge for payment acceptance the way a card acquirer could.

Internationally, Saathi had two exposures. Meenakshi Sundaram ran a customer-success team in Singapore piloting the product with sundry shops in Malaysia and Indonesia, where the ledger translated well and the B2B ordering network did not exist. And Gregory Fernandes, hired in New Jersey in 2025, was selling a stripped-down English version to independent convenience stores in the United States, a market where the attention line had no equivalent because no consumer brand wanted to reach 900 stores through an app.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence from April to October 2026 is worth setting out precisely, because the beliefs changed faster than the evidence.

In April, sponsored content launched in the Feed on the strength of counsel's opinion. The belief was that a clearly marked Sponsored tab was categorically different from an ad in a ledger, and that retailers would treat festive merchandising videos from a brand they already stocked as useful rather than intrusive. Early data supported this: completion rates on sponsored videos were 61 percent, higher than on Saathi's own educational content.

In June, a media agency called Vistaar assembled a consortium of FMCG advertisers and proposed an annual inventory commitment: ₹210 crore over FY27 and FY28 against guaranteed impressions and category exclusivity in three categories. The belief in the commercial team was that this validated a new business. The term sheet is Exhibit 5. One clause — the remedy if Saathi under-delivers impressions — is marked "to be finalised".

In July, Rhea Bhattacharya's team changed the definition of a weekly active retailer to include app opens that touched only the Feed. The reason given was that the old definition, which required a billing or ledger event, understated engagement. The change was noted in a release ticket and not in the metrics dictionary. Every "weekly retention" figure in the board pack after July is computed on the new definition, and the figure for March, used as the comparison base, is not.

In August, field sales in Pune and Coimbatore began reporting a pattern their regional managers described as "clause 4.3 questions": retailers asking, on renewal calls, whether the brand videos meant the company was now selling their data. Renewal conversion on those calls fell from 79 percent to 74 percent in the two zones where sponsored content density was highest. The belief in the sales organisation hardened into conviction: the Feed was costing renewals. Ananya's view was that the two zones were also the two zones where a competitor had run a price promotion in July.

In September, two things arrived within a week. Ananya's decile analysis (Exhibit 4) showed renewal falling with Feed exposure. And a retailer survey commissioned from a Pune research agency (Exhibit 6) reported that 71 percent of retailers found the brand videos "useful or very useful". The survey and the decile analysis are both in the board pack, on consecutive pages, with no comment reconciling them.

What has turned out to be wrong: the 2024 take-rate assumption, the 2025 churn business case, and — Shalini increasingly suspects, though she cannot prove it — the July definition change, which has made every engagement number in the pack incomparable with its own history at exactly the moment the company is using those numbers to choose what kind of company it is.

5. The people

Shalini Deshmukh, chief product officer, Bengaluru. Position: not yet stated. Incentive: her FY27 bonus is 40 percent weighted to "product-led revenue growth", a term the compensation committee defined loosely enough to include ad revenue. Not saying: she wrote clause 4.3 herself and has begun to wonder whether she is defending retailers or defending her own past decision.

Devendra Kulkarni, founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: build around the ad line; it is the only line with venture-scale margins. Incentive: a Series D conversation with a growth fund that has asked, twice, about "the retail media opportunity". Not saying: the indicative valuation he has been quoted assumes the Vistaar commitment is signed.

Rhea Bhattacharya, senior vice-president of growth, Bengaluru. Position: the North Star should be monthly reached retailers, because reach is what advertisers buy and because the Feed is the only thing in the company growing faster than 20 percent. Incentive: her team's objectives are minutes and monthly actives; she proposed the July definition change. Not saying: she thinks the ledger business is a mature annuity that will never grow again, and that saying so out loud would be career-limiting with Farhan on the leadership team.

Farhan Shaikh, co-founder and vice-president of engineering, Pune. Position: the company is a productivity product and should say so; video in a bandwidth-constrained offline-first app is architecturally corrosive and has already pushed the median app size from 24 MB to 71 MB. Incentive: 130 of his 190 engineers work on the ledger and ordering stack. Not saying: he is personally offended by the sponsored content, having sold clause 4.3 in Marathi to shopkeepers himself in 2023.

Dr Ananya Ghosh, head of data science, Toronto. Position: nobody should choose a North Star on the current evidence; the decile analysis is confounded and the survey instrument is leading. Incentive: professional credibility; she has signed her name to Exhibit 4's caveats. Not saying: she has run a cleaner matched analysis on a 40,000-retailer subsample and the result is ambiguous — a 1.1-point renewal difference with a confidence interval that crosses zero — and she has not put it in the pack because she is not sure whether an ambiguous result would be used to justify proceeding.

Lena Brandt, principal designer, Berlin. Position: the Feed as currently designed is a violation of the promise in spirit, and the notification that opens it at 9 a.m. is a dark pattern. Incentive: her design team's charter is trust and accessibility. Not saying: she wrote directly to Devendra on 20 September, copying nobody, and has not told Shalini.

Meenakshi Sundaram, head of customer success, Singapore. Position: the North Star must count completed work — invoices raised, books closed, stock counted — because that is what her Malaysian and Indonesian pilots buy and because there is no ad market there. Incentive: her FY27 target is 4,000 paying shops in Southeast Asia. Not saying: she is at 1,150 in month seven and behind plan, and a productivity North Star would make her the most important person in the company rather than the most exposed.

Gregory Fernandes, head of sales, New Jersey. Position: the marketplace is the real business; take rates rise with volume and the US convenience-store market would pay for ordering. Incentive: commission on new bookings. Not saying: two-thirds of his pipeline is resellers rather than end stores, and the reseller deals carry a support obligation nobody has costed.

Rashid Al Owais, group operations director of Barakah Grocers, Dubai — a customer, not an employee, running 61 supermarkets across the UAE and negotiating an ₹18 crore three-year white-label deal. Position: he will sign only if the contract states that no third-party advertising appears in any Barakah-branded instance. Not saying: he is also in conversation with one of Saathi's competitors.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the exhibit Devendra reads. Read naively, it says the ad line is growing eight-fold and produces gross profit second only to subscription. Read with its footnote, it says something weaker: one quarter, annualised, with a quarter of that quarter's revenue booked for delivery in a festive window that has not happened yet and whose accounting treatment is unsettled. Exhibit 2 is the exhibit that makes the framing question hard rather than easy. The segment that spends the most time in the Feed — ledger-only shops, 2.11 lakh of them — pays the least, at ₹760 a shop a year, and is only 19 percent paid. The segment that pays the most spends the least time in the Feed. If the company's customers are the shops, attention and revenue are inversely related here. If the company's customers are the advertisers, then 2.11 lakh engaged shop owners are the most valuable asset in the table and their unwillingness to pay ₹3,499 is irrelevant.

The two exhibits cannot both be taken at face value, and neither can be dismissed. Exhibit 3's retention rise is partly an artefact of counting Feed-only opens as activity — a definition under which a shop owner who stopped billing entirely but watches videos each morning has become more retained. Exhibit 4's renewal decline is partly an artefact of who is in the top deciles. Between them lies Ananya's unpublished matched analysis, which nobody in the room on Monday will know exists.

8. The options as Shalini currently sees them

Option A. Declare the productivity game. North Star: daily billing shops — shops recording a sale or invoice on a given day. Keep the Feed educational, drop sponsored content, decline Vistaar, sign Barakah, put the squad on GST e-invoicing and stock counting. Upside: it is proportional to 70 percent of gross profit, it honours clause 4.3, it is the same product in Johor as in Jhunjhunu, and it is what the paying segment does. Cost: forgoes ₹84 crore of FY27 revenue at 91 percent margin, tells the fastest-growing team in the company that their work does not count, and asks the board to accept 13 percent growth in a market that rewards 40.

Option B. Declare the transaction game. North Star: weekly ordering shops, or B2B gross merchandise value. Upside: it is the only line with a structural network effect, Gregory's US market would pay for it, and it makes Saathi a participant in ONDC rather than an app. Cost: a 1.8 percent take rate against competitors with warehouses and working capital, 34 percent gross margin, and no evidence Saathi can move the rate.

Option C. Declare the attention game. North Star: monthly reached retailers. Sign Vistaar, build the consent flow, amend clause 4.3 with notice. Upside: the margin, the growth rate, the fund conversation. Cost: a six-week consent programme that re-opens the promise in public, the Barakah deal, probably Farhan and Lena, and a business in which 2.11 lakh shops that pay ₹760 a year become the asset while the shops paying ₹5,880 become secondary.

Shalini's difficulty, sitting at the dining table, is that all three options answer the question "which game are we playing?" and she has begun to suspect that the question is wrong, or at least incomplete. Each option assumes the company has one customer. Under Option C the customer is the advertiser and the retailer is inventory; under Option A the customer is the shop; under Option B the customer is arguably the distributor. The three games may not be three strategies for one business but three businesses wearing one app. Nor does any option ask whether the game differs by segment — daily billers may be a productivity business and ledger-only shops an attention business, in which case a single North Star for 4.2 lakh shops is the thing that cannot survive. And Ananya's fourth box, aggregate demand data sold to brands as a subscription, would let Saathi sell to brands without showing a retailer a single advertisement, which is either the elegant answer or a DPDP problem with a nicer name.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10 a.m. on Monday, 5 October. The Vistaar signature window closes on 31 October and the festive flight requires live inventory by 20 October; Diwali falls on 8 November. Barakah's signature window is described by Rashid as "this month". The DPDP consent re-collection, if Option C proceeds, takes six weeks by legal's estimate, which puts completion after the festive flight it is meant to enable. Amending clause 4.3 requires 30 days' notice to every paid subscriber in eleven languages.

Cash: ₹680 crore on the balance sheet, 19 months of runway at the current burn of ₹36 crore a quarter. People: Farhan has one uncommitted squad of eleven engineers for Q3, and video infrastructure, the consent flow, and GST e-invoicing each need that squad entirely. Contracts: the 2025 distributor agreements that underpin the ordering marketplace contain a clause giving distributors the right to review "any promotional surface" in the app, which nobody has yet read against the Vistaar exclusivity terms. And the compensation plans for 340 employees, including Rhea's team, were set in April against metrics that Option A would make irrelevant.

11. Half past one

At half past one, Shalini went back through the three versions of slide seven and noticed something she had not intended. In the first version, the number counted shops. In the second, it counted orders. In the third, it counted retailers reached — and the word she had typed without thinking was not "customers" but "retailers", because in that version they were not the customers.

She thought about the man in Kolhapur that Farhan kept bringing up, who had asked three times. She thought about Ananya's sentence — I cannot give you one by Monday — and about the ₹84 crore, and about the eleven engineers who could do exactly one of three things. She opened a fourth blank slide, typed "What if the answer is that we are two companies", looked at it for a while, and did not know whether it was the most important thing she had written all weekend or an elaborate way of avoiding a decision that was due in eight and a half hours.

She left all four slides in the deck and went to bed.
